reviews.text:
I went to pray today, and at first I wasn’t allowed to come in. That honestly felt confusing and hurtful. A little later, a woman who told me she was a member of the board came over and asked who I was and what I was doing there. I understand that people may want to look after the mosque, but the way it happened made me feel like I didn’t belong.

I’m sharing this from the heart, because a mosque is supposed to be a place where Muslims feel welcome, regardless of where they come from. I’ve even experienced churches while traveling that were happy to welcome me as a Muslim and let me pray, so it’s difficult when I come to a mosque and feel like I’m being questioned simply for wanting to pray.

I also want to mention Friday khutbahs. I respect the Bosnian community and the history of the mosque, but I’ve noticed that the khutbah is mostly in Bosnian. Since we live in Canada and the mosque welcomes Muslims from different backgrounds, I think having the main khutbah in English, with Bosnian or Arabic included if needed, would help everyone understand and feel included.

I’m not writing this to attack anyone. I genuinely like having a mosque like this in the community, and I hope these things can improve. A mosque is the house of Allah, and every Muslim who comes sincerely to pray should feel that there is a place for them.

reviews.name: Leo Avci
reviews.text:
I’ve tried to overlook this for the past 2–3 months because I truly appreciate the Imam’s effort and understand that he is doing his best. However, after attending a few other mosques, the difference in the quality of the khutbahs became much more noticeable.

Unfortunately, I feel this is something that needs to improve. The khutbah should ideally be delivered by someone who is more comfortable and fluent in English, but more importantly, the topics should be meaningful, thought-provoking, and help strengthen people’s faith.

Every week, a lot is said during the 30–40 minute khutbah, but I often leave without really understanding what the main message or takeaway was. Unfortunately, I know I’m not the only person who feels this way. At times, it seems that people are simply waiting for the khutbah to finish rather than being engaged by it.

Please don’t take this as an attack or an attempt to criticize anyone personally. I respect the effort being made and genuinely want this mosque to succeed. People come to the mosque hoping to listen, learn, reflect, and leave with stronger faith. I believe improving the khutbah would make a significant difference for the community.

UPDATE – Response to the owner:

I’ve mostly been attending the 2:30 PM prayer because of the parking situation. I really don’t mean to criticize the imam personally, and I appreciate everyone volunteering for the second prayer. My only concern is that I don’t find the topics are delivered as effectively as they could be. Maybe it’s just my personal preference though, so I’ve increased my rating to 4 stars to be fair.

Since both shifts differ in their delivery style and focus, knowing which specific Khutbah you attended will help us review the situation better and work directly on making the necessary improvements.

I am deeply disappointed with my experience at this mosque. As a Pakistani Hazara, I have often felt unwelcome due to the behavior of certain individuals, particularly some of the women, whose treatment has come across as discriminatory and exclusionary.

What hurts most is that a mosque should be a place where all believers are treated with dignity and respect, regardless of ethnicity or background. Unfortunately, that has not been my experience here.

During Muharram nights, there have been occasions when, instead of simply serving niyaz to attendees, people would ask, “You don’t want niyaz, right?” This feels dismissive and unwelcoming. Niyaz is traditionally offered with generosity and respect, not in a way that makes someone feel singled out or uncomfortable.

I understand that a mosque belongs to Allah and not to any individual or group. However, self-respect also matters. Rather than continue attending a place where I feel unwelcome, I choose to drive farther to a mosque where I am treated with kindness and equality.

I sincerely hope the leadership reflects on these issues and works toward creating an environment where everyone feels respected, included, and valued.

reviews.text:
Tragically, I used to like coming to the Masjid and praying. It felt nice praying the Asr and Maghrib prayers just before going home but the Masjid is nothing but the owner's bedroom.

He allows what he wants, prevents what he wants and runs the Masjid against the Sunnah of Prophet Muhammad peace and blessings be upon Him.

I used to put money here and I stopped. They care more about money than they do about the place and you can see it in their eyes and faces. The parking lot only features their high-end cars. Bought for free by the money of the people. Gut-wrenching...

And I wish they paid enough respect and significance to the people and made them feel welcomed and respected as they come in, wanting to spend time with Allah, as they did to themselves and their personal glamour.

It always feels like you are being watched and there is a brother who always makes you feel this way. I came in once and he stood just staring me down as if I was something undeserving in his sight... He stood behind me, walked closer in front of me and kept watching me all over until I finished my prayer...

The owner of this place likes to believe it "belongs" to him because he built it. Shake my head... What a disgusting mentality to live by as a Muslim. Truly, what a disgusting mentality.

They run a ginormous business inside the Masjid. They also seem very well-off and it came to my knowledge one of their owners owns a very successful gas station. Allah knows best if it is the owner or not, but really, putting money here feels like it is more money in a rich mans pocket. And as a Musalli, you get nothing in return.

Keep your money brothers and sisters from this Masjid.

He also has a HUGE sign posted inside saying, "there is no prayer in congregation after the main congregation" in bold lettering. And the sign feels like it was posted by a tyrant running a show.

What kind of Sunnah is this? This is a blatant rejection and "Kufr"—disbelief of the Prophetic way of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him. Unambiguously it is against the Sahih Ahadith for prayers to be done in congregation, of which the Prophet ordered for—for the sake of the Ummah and its unity. As well as the 27 degrees higher of a reward affixed for congregational prayers which is narrated in a Sahih—authentic Hadith.

Additionally, it is a crime against the Sunnah because prayers must always be offered when the time comes in. The congregation can be before or after the main one, depending on the person's circumstances. You can make your own Jama'ah if brothers walk-in and want to pray, or sisters to themselves likewise.

Most of the time you walk in, you will find a group of bearded men who run this Masjid, sitting down in a room with the door open and situated very close to the sister's section. They are also in parameter of the main entrance of the Masjid and the prayer sanctuary too. You will see them laughing in between prayers out loud and playing a table board game that involves shooting discs across a board, even as brothers and sisters are praying...

What the Hell is this? What kind of Ummah have we become?

You walk in and it feels like a Shisha lounge...

Fear Allah and conceal it away from the sanctity of the prayer sanctuary. Fear Allah and dedicate a respectable place for entertainment that everyone can engage in too. Not your gangster circle alone...

Then you walk in to the prayer sanctuary and brightly coloured carpets of luxury-feel are laid down every single day for every 5 daily prayers, so the management and their top inner circle of religious "Imams" get the first row behind the Imam. And the Imam is the same guy from within that very same circle...

May Allah guide the people here. They are truly not representatives of Islam in a pure and non-hypocritical way. The moment you walk in, I swear to you by Allah, you feel hypocrisy at the door... And you just don't feel good within yourself or altogether, so long as you are inside, and in confrontation with the operators of this place. Very sad scenes, I swear by Allah, for one to see...

reviews.responseFromOwnerText:
Assalamualaikum sister, we are sorry to disappoint you for the experience. I do want to clarify few concerns you have mentioned but I will also bring up your concern to prevent this happening in future inshallah. 

The mosque is fully volunteered run, we do not have on-site staff so there are days where the volunteer may forget to open the door on sister side. The brother side is open most of the time due to local foot traffic going on/off whereas the sister side gets locked due to safety after prayer time. We have encountered many troubling situation before where we had unexpected entrance (from any entrance) but its easier from sister-end due less foot traffic. This is not an excuse, we will look into why sister side is not opened.

The mosque in general is going thru renovation, you are only seeing the sister side but even on the men side beside the clock we have materials out in open while we work on this. The renovations and cleaning are all volunteer run too.

We take our commitment to health and safety very seriously, we will make sure to figure out why there are smells coming from bathroom. The bathrooms are cleaned daily before closing by volunteers. 

We are a small volunteer led community working hard to improve our facilities, but your feedback highlights areas where we must do better. We pray Allah rewards you for bringing this to our attention, and we warmly invite you to visit us again soon to experience the improvements firsthand.

Jazakillahu Khayran

فَبِمَا رَحْمَةٍ مِّنَ اللَّهِ لِنتَ لَهُمْ ۖ وَلَوْ كُنتَ فَظًّا غَلِيظَ الْقَلْبِ لَانفَضُّوا مِنْ حَوْلِكَ ۖ فَاعْفُ عَنْهُمْ وَاسْتَغْفِرْ لَهُمْ وَشَاوِرْهُمْ فِي الْأَمْرِ ۖ فَإِذَا عَزَمْتَ فَتَوَكَّلْ عَلَى اللَّهِ ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ يُحِبُّ الْمُتَوَكِّلِينَ
— Surah Ali 'Imran, 3:159
This matters even more with our youth, who already face so much misinformation online. They deserve correction delivered with a smile and with respect, not yelling.

After the prayer, once most people had left, I approached him privately and told him what he did was wrong — that as an Imam, he should have met the young brother with kindness and guided him gently instead of reacting with aggression. Rather than reflect on this, he raised his voice at me too, insisted he had done nothing wrong, and asked me to leave the masjid. Allah describes the people He loves this way:
"الَّذِينَ يُنفِقُونَ فِي السَّرَّاءِ وَالضَّرَّاءِ وَالْكَاظِمِينَ الْغَيْظَ وَالْعَافِينَ عَنِ النَّاسِ ۗ وَاللَّهُ يُحِبُّ الْمُحْسِنِينَ" — Surah Ali 'Imran, 3:134

I was honestly stunned that this was how an Imam chose to respond. This didn't affect only me. Several of us were distracted during the prayer, still thinking about what had just happened, and I personally had to repeat my Asr afterward. Having an Imam who doesn't understand what our youth are up against today, or how to take their hand and guide them toward the right path with patience, is a disgrace to this community. Allah instructs us:
"ادْعُ إِلَىٰ سَبِيلِ رَبِّكَ بِالْحِكْمَةِ وَالْمَوْعِظَةِ الْحَسَنَةِ ۖ وَجَادِلْهُم بِالَّتِي هِيَ أَحْسَنُ ۚ إِنَّ رَبَّكَ هُوَ أَعْلَمُ بِمَن ضَلَّ عَن سَبِيلِهِ ۖ وَهُوَ أَعْلَمُ بِالْمُهْتَدِينَ"— Surah An-Nahl, 16:125

Whether the young brother was right or wrong in whatever he did barely matters now — the way he was spoken to was harsh enough to make him resent ever setting foot in the masjid again. Even Musa and Harun, sent to confront Pharaoh, one of the most tyrannical men in history, were commanded:
"فَقُولَا لَهُ قَوْلًا لَّيِّنًا لَّعَلَّهُ يَتَذَكَّرُ أَوْ يَخْشَىٰ"— Surah Taha, 20:44
If Allah asked for gentleness even toward Pharaoh, a struggling young Muslim deserves nothing less.

I will not be returning to this masjid, nor will I continue to support it. I ask the community and board members to take this matter seriously. Allah says:
"وَلْتَكُن مِّنكُمْ أُمَّةٌ يَدْعُونَ إِلَى الْخَيْرِ وَيَأْمُرُونَ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ وَيَنْهَوْنَ عَنِ الْمُنكَرِ ۚ وَأُولَـٰئِكَ هُمُ الْمُفْلِحُونَ"— Surah Ali 'Imran, 3:104

If this masjid's true purpose is to help and guide our youth — who are the future of this Ummah — then this cannot be brushed aside.

reviews.name: Adriana Gobeti Gil
reviews.text:
Assalamu Alaikum
Sher, I want to start by saying that I really love this place. I love coming to this mosque, and I have a lot of respect and affection for you as a brother. But regarding the words that were spoken yesterday, I completely disagree with what was said.
There is something that really bothered me about what the imam said yesterday, especially regarding people who have dogs and spend money taking care of them.
First of all, I believe that having a dog can be a blessing from God, and I want to explain why. I am not talking about giving dogs properties or putting property in their names. I am talking about taking care of them, feeding them, providing medical care when necessary, and giving them the same love and affection that they give us.
And there is something else that I think is important to remember. During the time of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, dogs were also present around the mosque. There is an authentic hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reporting that, during the Prophet’s lifetime, dogs used to enter and leave the mosque. The narration even mentions that they urinated inside it, and there was no order to wash the mosque because of that. This shows me that we need to be careful not to make the issue of dogs into something bigger than what is actually established in the Islamic teachings.
I am not saying that we should ignore the Islamic teachings concerning dogs. I know there are hadiths about keeping dogs, and I understand that scholars have different explanations regarding the circumstances and rulings surrounding them. But I believe we should look at the complete picture and not use only one aspect of the teachings to make people feel guilty or judged for loving and caring for an animal.
Dogs give so much to human beings. They save lives in situations that are often created by human beings themselves. They are trained to find people trapped under rubble, locate survivors, find missing people, detect danger, and assist during wars and disasters.
And it is not only that. Dogs also help people who are going through difficult emotional situations. Many people who struggle with loneliness, anxiety, depression, or trauma find comfort and companionship in their dogs.
A dog loves you without asking for anything in return. When you come home, your dog welcomes you as if you had been away for years. A dog is loyal, affectionate, and always there for you.
So when someone says that people should not spend money on their dogs, I think we need to look at the bigger picture. If someone has the financial means to properly feed their dog, care for them, take them to the veterinarian, and provide them with a safe and healthy life, I don’t understand why showing compassion and responsibility toward an animal that completely depends on us should automatically be viewed as something negative.
In fact, I believe there is something much more serious that we should talk about: abandoning an animal after taking responsibility for it.
If someone chooses to adopt or buy a pet, they are taking on a responsibility. Taking a dog, creating a bond with that animal, and then simply abandoning it on the street, leaving it without proper food, water, shelter, or protection, is something that concerns me much more than someone spending money to properly care for their pet.
If we are going to talk about mercy, responsibility, and what is sinful, then we should also talk about not abusing or abandoning a creature of God that depends on human beings for its survival.
An animal feels hunger, thirst, fear, and pain. It did not choose to be on the street, and it cannot protect or care for itself in the same way a human being can.
So, in my opinion, if we want to teach people about Islamic responsibility toward animals, we should not only talk about what is permissible or prohibited regarding having a dog. We should also talk about the responsibility to treat animals with mercy and not to abandon, abuse, or neglect them.
For me, compassion, honesty, loyalty, and responsibility should be taught together.

ownerDescription:
Uthman Mosque is a peaceful place of worship and a welcoming community center located on Dawes Road in East York, Toronto. We offer five daily prayers and Jumu’ah (Friday) prayer in a clean, respectful, and friendly environment.
During the blessed month of Ramadan, free Iftar is provided for everyone in the community. The mosque also offers free parking for visitors and a separate prayer area for women to ensure comfort and convenience for all worshippers.
Our mission is to promote unity, faith, and community service while providing a safe and spiritually uplifting space for all. Everyone is warmly welcome.
